source.title: The Algorithm Is Not the Behavior: Learned Priors Override Look-Ahead in a Chess-Playing Neural Network
source.authors: E. Sandmann; S. Lapuschkin; W. Samek

page_placements.theme: Decision-relevant state and policy across layers in chess and agentic models (state tracking, not shown look-ahead)

record.tranche_reason: The study measures layer-wise chess policies and puzzle choices, reporting that correct moves can appear and later be displaced, and that some move preferences reflect heuristics. It does not causally intervene on a look-ahead feature.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates layer-wise chess policies and reports results relevant to the stability and interpretation of apparent plans. Its references to the L12H12 look-ahead head are attributed to Jenner et al. (2024), not results tested here. Playing-strength and puzzle-solving results are recorded only where they bear on the reported policy dynamics; cited results are not included.
record.test_reason: The study applies a Post-LN logit lens to Leela's policy network and tracks how the current-move distribution evolves across layers (rank correlation, JS divergence, puzzle solve rates). It never measures a representation of future moves or tokens and never intervenes on one, so it does not test look-ahead. Its link to look-ahead is interpretive only. It says the sharp change at layer 12 aligns with Jenner et al.'s L12H12 look-ahead head, and that one late jump 'may indicate' multi-move analysis. Its heuristic explanations (queen-check bias, material-gain bias) concern which immediate move intermediate layers prefer, not whether a plan is shallow. That is iterative inference over the next action, a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find monotonic gains in playing strength and puzzle solving across layers, but non-smooth policy trajectories, unlike the smooth convergence seen in language models. They propose middle-layer feature engineering followed by late residual sharpening. They note that the sharp layer-12 inflection aligns with Jenner et al.'s look-ahead head (cited, not tested here). Their stated limitation is that the Post-LN focus makes domain and architecture effects hard to disentangle.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a Post-LN logit-lens extension and layer-wise chess policy measurements, rather than rhyme-prompt probing and causal interventions on candidate rhyme words.
record.method_sensitivity: Puzzle-specific trajectories differ: some winning moves appear early and persist, while others are displaced or emerge late. Ranking correlation rises sharply around layer 12.

fits_no_version.finding: In Leela T82, the logit-lens policy reorders move preferences until late layers: Kendall tau stays low until about layer 12 and JS divergence stays high. Correct puzzle moves are often found and then discarded. This contrasts with near-linear rank convergence in GPT-2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterative inference in chess transformers is non-monotonic at the policy level, even though playing strength rises monotonically with depth.

record.problems: Evidence is based on one chess model and layer-wise logit-lens measurements, not causal interventions on the proposed features. Several aggregate metric values are presented only in figures; individual puzzle examples do not establish how representative their trajectories are. The authors note that the focus on a Post-LN architecture makes domain- and architecture-specific explanations difficult to disentangle.
record.rows_left_out: Playing-strength results, general puzzle solve rates by Elo, entropy, final-top-move probability, and MLP output norms were not separately recorded where they did not directly measure the instability or heuristic explanations relevant to V6. GPT-2 comparisons are not evidence for the claim versions tested here.

untested.parts: All; no verse or LLM rhyme analysis.
All; no decoding of moves or tokens several steps ahead.
All; no test of features computed for later positions.
Chess look-ahead is referenced only through Jenner et al.; no future-move probe or intervention is run here.
No measure of how far ahead any plan reaches, or whether it steers output. Heuristic claims concern immediate-move preferences only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked every row to V6 and labelled it 'supports'. That is not warranted: the heuristic explanations concern which immediate move intermediate layers prefer, not whether plans are shallow or incidental. The study is not a test of any version. The GPT-2 comparison and the Elo tables are likewise unrelated to planning ahead.

versions.untested_parts: Rhyme-word representations before verse lines and causal interventions that change the line.
Decoding tokens several positions ahead from a single hidden state.
Whether features are computed for later positions rather than as a side effect of next-token prediction.
Rhyme planning in open-weight models or open attribution/probing tools.
The study does not directly measure or intervene on look-ahead in chess; it does not test other tasks or architectures such as multi-step reasoning or Sokoban.

The study does not establish causal effects of candidate-move representations on later moves, quantify how many moves ahead any representation reaches, or compare performance with a causal intervention that removes the proposed planning feature.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.operation_detail: Measured Kendall’s τ between intermediate and final move rankings over 1000 CCRL positions.
rows.value: Correlation is negative in early layers, remains low through middle layers, and increases sharply around layer 12.
rows.uncertainty: 5th–95th and 25th–75th percentile ranges shown; exact values not stated in text.
rows.note: The text describes substantial reordering of move preferences until late layers; it does not identify a cause or establish whether this is causal planning.
rows.check: Kendall's tau between intermediate-layer and final current-move rankings measures layer-wise convergence of the next-move policy, not look-ahead depth or whether a plan steers output. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.operation_detail: Measured Kendall’s τ between intermediate and final move rankings over 1000 CCRL positions, restricting the ranking to moves appearing in the top 5 at any layer.

conditions.value: moves appearing in the top 5 at any layer

rows.value: Correlation is negative in early layers and remains low until around layer 12, then increases sharply; some positions have rankings similar to or dissimilar from the final ranking until late in the network.
rows.uncertainty: 5th–95th and 25th–75th percentile ranges shown; exact values not stated in text.
rows.note: Shows late changes in rankings, but does not demonstrate that an apparent plan is unused or causally steers generation.
rows.check: Same construct as R1 (top-5 variant). It measures next-move ranking convergence, not planning.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.2, Figure 6b and accompanying paragraph.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.operation_detail: Measured Jensen–Shannon divergence between layer policies and the final policy over 1000 CCRL positions.
rows.value: Median divergence remains high until the final layers; the 5th percentile is much lower, indicating that a small subset of positions converges early while most have different move preferences through most layers.
rows.uncertainty: 5th–95th and 25th–75th percentile ranges shown; exact values not stated in text.
rows.locator: Appendix C.1, Figure 5a and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors describe position-dependent convergence; the measure alone does not test causal steering.
rows.check: JS divergence to the final policy measures distributional convergence across depth, not future-move representation.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.1, Figure 5a and Jensen-Shannon divergence paragraph.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise, cumulative, converged, and first-discovered puzzle solutions.
rows.value: Solutions are frequently discovered and subsequently discarded; new solution discovery is highest in initial and final layers and lower in the middle; final cumulative solve rate exceeds final-layer performance.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes these patterns, but the plotted rates are not given numerically in the text.
rows.check: Puzzle solutions discovered and then discarded across layers concern the argmax current move. They say nothing about whether future moves are represented.

source_check.locator_found: §2.3, puzzle evaluation; §3.2, puzzle solution stability and Figure 3.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.operation_detail: Tracked policy probabilities for the winning move Ng3+ and competing moves across layers on the Figure 1 puzzle.
rows.measure: Probability assigned to the winning move and competing move probabilities
rows.value: Ng3+ is 21.09% at layer 5, is overtaken by Qg1+ across layers 6–10, and reaches 47.38% at layer 13 and 87.55% in the final output; Rh6 is 54.15% at layer 12. The authors suggest the Qg1+ preference reflects a learned queen-check heuristic.
rows.locator: Appendix E, Tables 4–5 and accompanying text
rows.note: The report shows non-monotonic preference and a proposed heuristic explanation; no intervention tests whether the candidate move representation steers intermediate text.
rows.check: Single-puzzle trajectory of current-move probabilities. The queen-check heuristic is the authors' speculation about an intermediate preference, not a test of plan depth.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix E, opening paragraph and Tables 4–5.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.operation_detail: Tracked policy probabilities for the winning move Nd6+ across layers on a puzzle.
rows.measure: Probability assigned to the winning move
rows.value: Nd6+ is 2.77% at layer 12, rises to 26.23% at layer 13, and becomes the decisive top choice in the final output.
rows.locator: Appendix F.1, Tables 6–7 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors connect the late rise to possible multi-move analysis, but do not test that explanation causally.
rows.check: Single puzzle. The link to the look-ahead head is speculative ('may indicate'), and no future-move representation is measured.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.operation_detail: Tracked policy probabilities for the winning move QXe8+ across layers on a puzzle.
rows.measure: Probability assigned to the winning move and leading competitor
rows.value: QXe8+ is the top candidate from layer 0 and remains so throughout, except for brief competition from bXc3 at layer 7 (50.8% vs 46.1%). The authors suggest early convergence may result from queen and capture biases.
rows.locator: Appendix F.2, Tables 8–9 and accompanying text
rows.note: Stable preference is consistent with early lock-in, while the authors offer a heuristic explanation; no causal test distinguishes these accounts.
rows.check: Single puzzle showing early lock-in of the current move. It does not bear on look-ahead.

rows.subject: T82-768x15x24h
rows.operation_detail: Tracked policy probabilities for the winning move Bh2+ and the competing material-gain move RXe3 across layers on a puzzle.
rows.value: The model favors RXe3 through layer 11; Bh2+ gains probability gradually from layer 5 and becomes the top choice after layer 12. The authors describe this as a late override of a simple material-gain heuristic.
rows.locator: Appendix F.5, Tables 14–15 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors interpret the trajectory in heuristic terms; no causal intervention tests that interpretation.
rows.check: Single puzzle. The 'override of material-gain heuristic' is an interpretation of current-move preferences, not a test of planning.

relation.reason: The discussion connects the layer-12 inflection to previously reported look-ahead circuitry; that connection is not tested here.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure current-move policy convergence across layers. They do not measure future-move representations or test whether an internal plan steers output.
